name: Liam Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal day on site involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and fit floor joists and boards on building sites, alongside general carpentry. I have a trade certificate, enough years behind me to work steadily, and no claim to being the best carpenter in town. I use AI now and then to check a materials count after another crew has tried it. My partner and I have grown children and a few months of expenses saved; I hope to leave regular site work at sixty-five in 2033 if our income covers the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger carpenters that a quick count is fine, but the joist still needs a proper bearing. An AI floor plan will not catch a loose joist hanger on a building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the usual wage to continue until the age-sixty-five target I have in mind. We have one to six months of bills saved and some similar jobs nearby, but my partner and I still need to check retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting joists and checking hangers by hand. I would use the occasional AI count as before, and sit with my partner to compare expected age-sixty-five income with our actual monthly bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work in this picture. My main uncertainty is whether we can afford the retirement date we already wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets checked after the joist count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every bearing and hanger on the built wall, especially near a stair opening. A correct number of joists can still make a bad floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would checking the retirement figures mean giving notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We would first compare expected income with housing and everyday costs. I would stay on the paid crew until those numbers work.

I would **use** the familiar count tool only alongside physical checks.
think: My **usual** wage looks safe, but retirement at sixty-five needs a household calculation.
A **few** months saved do not replace steady income.
do: **Keep** fitting joists and checking hangers on paid site shifts.
**Compare** expected age-sixty-five retirement income with our actual housing, food and repair bills together.
feel: **Calm** about current work, cautious about retirement affordability.
S0.quote: An AI floor plan will not catch a loose joist hanger on a building site.
fieldNote: **Liam** uses AI occasionally for counts and relies on physical joist checks.
His **retirement** target is sixty-five in 2033, conditional on household income rather than a response to AI.

steps.text: Keep fitting and checking building-site joists
Check age-sixty-five retirement figures before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say quicker office buying could get joists to the site on time, if the supplier and builder use the same measurements. I would learn a new AI delivery check after another crew proves it catches missing hangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster AI delivery list could leave my joist crew with less paid waiting and a smaller retirement pot. My base fitting wage may hold, but any lost overtime would make the age-sixty-five plan less comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid joist shifts and compare delivery lists with the timber on two jobs. If the new AI check proves useful, I would practice it, then ask the builder for written paid-hour and rate terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible overtime loss, though the household has some savings and local work. I can test the tool without pretending a screen builds the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the delivery check useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The right joist lengths and hangers arrive before the crew is paid to fit them. I would compare the list with actual material on two jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change if overtime fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would rerun the retirement budget. If the loss became regular, I would apply to a posted nearby carpenter job only if the wage covered our bills.

I would **ask** how faster buying changes paid site hours and rates.
think: **Lost** overtime could weaken our planned age-sixty-five retirement budget.
**Some** savings and nearby roles let me respond without rushing into a bad offer.
do: **Compare** joist deliveries and paid hours on two building jobs.
**Practice** new AI delivery check if another crew proves it reliable.
**Apply** after regular cuts to posted local carpenter job with household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible own overtime loss, with practical options.
S1.quote: A faster AI delivery list could leave my joist crew with less paid waiting and a smaller retirement pot.
fieldNote: He **learns** new technology after practical proof, consistent with a steady rather than early-adopter profile.
**Possible** overtime loss matters because his retirement budget needs regular earnings, despite moderate savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches us in 2028 when I am sixty, but capable hands-on robots arrive around 2031 when I am sixty-three. A joist robot arriving at sixty-three could take two years of wages I still need before sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think standard joist fitting could lose paid shifts in those final two years. Our few months saved cannot replace two full wages, and I would rather earn than ask the grown children to fill the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the builder for written human fitting hours through 2031 and keep working. If robots cut shifts, I would apply to a posted local repair-carpentry job only if its wage covers our bills; I would delay optional house improvements until the income is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real two-year gap, but I can search among some nearby jobs. I would not claim early retirement unless the income actually covered it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair work could you still do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Replacing damaged floor sections in lived-in buildings, where each opening is different. I would need a posted nearby job and a wage figure before leaving the current crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What house improvement would wait first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone the planned garden paving. We would keep essential repairs and the monthly housing bill in the budget.

say: **Thinking** AI reaches site plans in 2028; fitting robots may reach joists in 2031.
I would **keep** earning toward sixty-five rather than assume I can stop at sixty-three.
think: A **few** months saved cannot cover two possible years of lost wages.
**Some** local repairs may offer work, but only an actual adequate vacancy would justify moving.
do: **Ask** builder for written joist-fitting hours through 2031.
**Delay** garden paving if robot fitting cuts paid shifts.
**Apply** after cuts to posted nearby repair job at household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage gap before planned retirement.
S2.quote: A joist robot arriving at sixty-three could take two years of wages I still need before sixty-five.
fieldNote: He **treats** the 2031 hands-on robot date as a possible two-year income gap before his existing target.
He **plans** to keep earning, cut optional spending after actual loss and require a posted local adequate job.

steps.text: Keep paid joist work while seeking written future hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three, and robots fit floors around 2034 when I am sixty-six. If our original age-sixty-five retirement in 2033 is affordable, robots arrive after I leave regular site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need to know whether the income covers our bills at sixty-five. If it does not, I could be working at sixty-six and would want some paid carpentry role rather than a training promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting joists now and check our expected income and monthly costs with my partner. If the figures support it, I would retire at the existing age-sixty-five target in 2033; otherwise I would keep paid work and apply only to posted local repair roles whose wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until we have checked the figures, but less threatened by this robot date. The floor robot of 2034 matters only if my retirement budget sends me back to site at sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you put in the calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Expected monthly income, housing, food and an allowance for repairs. If those costs beat the income, I will keep seeking paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course for a year or two of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the course was fully funded, the study days were paid and a posted local role paid enough for our bills. I would not enroll on the strength of an advert alone.

I would **retire** only if checked household income covers our bills.
think: If the **budget** fails, I may still need paid carpentry at sixty-six.
A **posted** local repair role with adequate pay is more useful than a vague course.
do: **Check** age-sixty-five household income and monthly costs with partner.
**Retire** at original 2033 target only if income covers ongoing bills.
**Apply** if still working to posted local repair job at household-covering wage.
S3.quote: The floor robot of 2034 matters only if my retirement budget sends me back to site at sixty-six.
fieldNote: His 2033 **target** predates the card; its actual exit remains conditional on sufficient income.

steps.text: Check age-sixty-five retirement income against household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI comes in 2036 when I am sixty-eight, and capable floor-fitting robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. A floor robot in 2039 cannot replace my pay if the household stopped needing it in 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not claim my future is settled until my partner and I see the income figures. If we cannot leave in 2033, I would keep fitting or repairing floors while my body and a builder will pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue the present paid joist shifts and review our age-sixty-five budget. If verified income covers ongoing costs, I would retire at that original target; if not, I would seek posted local repair work at a wage that pays the household, without claiming I will still be on site in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the machine timetable if our retirement figures work and uneasy until they do. The long lead time lets us decide from numbers rather than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to help you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and I would rather keep a paid carpentry job if our figures do not work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take a local repair role after sixty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted opening, a clear wage covering our bills and work I can do safely. I would not accept an informal promise just to stay busy.

say: The 2036 **thinking** change and 2039 robots likely follow my existing retirement target.
I would **continue** paid work only if checked income cannot cover household costs.
think: **Retirement** in 2033 is conditional; I cannot predict a site job at seventy-one.
**Some** nearby repair roles may help if household income remains short.
do: **Keep** paid joist work while checking 2033 retirement income.
**Retire** at original age-sixty-five target only if verified income covers bills.
**Apply** if income falls short to posted local repair role at adequate wage.
feel: **Calm** about distant robots if budget works, uneasy until verified.
S4.quote: A floor robot in 2039 cannot replace my pay if the household stopped needing it in 2033.
fieldNote: The **long** scenario does not assume Liam is still on site at seventy-one.
His **conditional** original retirement target is not early retirement; insufficient income leads to paid local work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because floor-fitting robots could arrive two years before my planned retirement. A written site-hours plan and a posted nearby repair role paying our bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the age-sixty-five budget has actually been checked. Until my partner and I see the figures, I will keep earning rather than call a hope a pension. I have a trade certificate for floors, not a certificate that our retirement bills will pay themselves.

headlineQuote: I have a trade certificate for floors, not a certificate that our retirement bills will pay themselves.
portrait: **Liam** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified construction worker who fits floor joists and boards.
He **has** typical wages, one to six months saved, a partner, grown children and some nearby jobs.
He **uses** AI occasionally after other crews prove a tool and values paid work over speculative promises.
He **hopes** to retire at sixty-five in 2033 if income covers bills; otherwise he seeks posted adequate local work.
biggestWorry: **Fast** floor-fitting robots around 2031 could cut wages two years before his hoped-for age-sixty-five retirement.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** paid site hours and a posted nearby repair job with household-covering pay would help.
